title: Is Point Lookout The Most Haunted Spot In Maryland? The Civil War Prison Site Says Yes

content:
At the very bottom tip of southern Maryland, a skinny finger of land splits the Potomac River from the Chesapeake Bay. Today it holds beaches, fishing piers, and quiet campsites.

During the Civil War, though, this same ground held a prison camp for Confederate soldiers, and that chapter has never really faded. Locals swap stories about strange happenings near the old lighthouse, and the place has earned a reputation as one of the spookiest corners of the state.

Yet families still swim, kayak, and crab here every summer without a second thought. So which is it, haunted history or peaceful getaway?

Keep reading to explore the past, the lighthouse, the water, the campgrounds, and the practical details you need before planning your own trip to this unusual waterfront park.

Where The River Meets The Bay

Maps make it look like Maryland simply runs out of room here. The peninsula narrows until water surrounds almost every side.

The spot is Point Lookout State Park, found at 11175 Point Lookout Rd, Scotland, MD 20687, United States. It sits in southern Maryland, where the Potomac River empties into the Chesapeake Bay.

That geography shapes everything about a visit. One side faces the bay and the other faces the river, so the views shift depending on which shore you choose.

The park is officially described as a recreational site built on the grounds of a former Civil War prison. Swimming, fishing, and camping are the main draws today.

Plenty of people treat it as a regular summer escape. Others come for the history and the eerie reputation that clings to the land.

Both groups tend to leave happy. The park holds a strong 4.5-star standing from more than 2,600 people who have shared their thoughts online, which is impressive for a place with such a heavy past.

Longtime fans call it their go-to stress relief, some for more than twenty years. That says a lot about how a site with such a serious backstory has become a calm retreat.

Before getting to the beaches, though, the story needs to start where the legends do.

A Prison Camp Chapter

Long before beach towels and fishing rods, this ground served a very different purpose. During the Civil War, it housed a prison camp for Confederate soldiers.

That fact is front and center in how the park presents itself. The official description calls it a recreational site on a Civil War prison, and history buffs make the trip specifically for that reason.

Civil War history comes up again and again when people talk about the park. Historical sites and markers are part of the experience, giving context to the open land you see today.

Many find the contrast striking. Families picnic and kids splash in the water on land that once held a far more somber scene.

The history is described as interesting and unique, and it adds weight to an otherwise easygoing day out. A stroll here can turn into an impromptu lesson.

Staff members are known for being kind and welcoming. They are a good resource if you want to understand what happened on these grounds.

This past is exactly why the park carries its haunted reputation. When a place holds so much history, stories tend to follow.

And few stories in Maryland get told as often as the ones tied to this shoreline.

Why The Ghost Stories Stick

Ask around southern Maryland about haunted places, and this park tends to come up quickly. The reason is simple: the prison camp history gives every legend a real foundation.

Ghost tales here are part of local folklore rather than official park attractions. The park itself focuses on recreation and history, so the spooky side is something people bring with them.

Still, the setting does its part. A remote tip of land, an old lighthouse, and water on almost every side create the kind of backdrop storytellers love.

Is it truly the most haunted spot in the state? That question has no official answer.

What can be said is that few Maryland parks pair such a deep Civil War connection with such a peaceful present. That tension is what keeps people curious.

Some arrive hoping for a goosebump moment near the lighthouse. Others simply want to understand the history behind the rumors.

Either way, the reputation adds an extra layer to a visit. It turns a beach day into something worth talking about on the drive home.

Speaking of the lighthouse, it deserves a closer look of its own.

The Lighthouse Everyone Talks About

Few landmarks on the property get as much attention as the lighthouse. It stands near the water and anchors the whole southern end of the park.

On open days, groups head up to the tower for a better look across the water. Windy afternoons are common, but that does not stop people from lining up for photos.

The building is described as beautiful inside. It also serves a practical role, since bottled water has been available for purchase there.

Views of the water around the lighthouse are a favorite. Many spend around an hour wandering the grounds, snapping pictures, and taking in the scene.

Even with plenty of families and groups around, the area rarely feels crowded. There is enough open space for everyone to find a corner.

The lighthouse is also central to the park’s eerie reputation. Its age and isolated position make it a natural focus for local legends.

For those with limited mobility, the area is a strong choice. Much can be seen from the car or with a short, easy walk.

Once the lighthouse is checked off the list, the beaches are calling.

Calm Water And Sandy Shores

Swimmers who dislike rough waves will find a friend here. The beaches are known for calm water that is clear and clean.

There are a couple of sandy beaches in the park, and they are often called ideal for wading or kayaking. Some consider this the best small beach in Maryland.

One heads-up: the water gets fairly deep. Even taller adults have found themselves standing on their tiptoes not far from shore.

A lifeguard has been seen patrolling the beach during busy times. That adds peace of mind for families with young swimmers.

Practical touches help too. Outdoor showers rinse off sand, and the bathroom facilities get positive mentions.

Restroom floors can stay wet from showers and constant foot traffic, so careful steps are wise. Shady trees near the picnic areas provide relief on hot days.

Grills are available, so there is no need to haul your own. That makes a full beach day much easier to plan.

Access to the beach is described as easy, even for those who cannot walk long distances. Just keep reading before you jump in, because the bay has a few residents worth knowing about.

Jellyfish, Dolphins, And Other Locals

Not every guest at the beach arrives by car. Jellyfish are a frequent topic of conversation, with more than forty mentions in online discussions about the park.

At certain times, there can be a lot of them. Swimming then becomes an at-your-own-risk decision.

Plenty of families turn it into entertainment instead. Watching jellyfish drift past from the fishing pier is a popular pastime for kids.

The wildlife list goes well beyond jellies. Fish, birds, and even dolphins have been spotted on the bay side.

Smaller critters deserve a mention as well. Sand flies, mosquitoes, and ticks can be part of the package, especially in marshy areas.

Bug spray and citronella are smart additions to any packing list. A quick tick check after hiking or camping is also a good habit.

None of this seems to keep people away. Most treat the wildlife, big and small, as part of the park’s natural character.

Spotting a dolphin fin while standing on Civil War ground is a combination few parks can offer. The next stop shows how to get even closer to the water.

Piers, Jetties, And Patient Anglers

Fishing ranks among the biggest reasons people make the trip. It shows up in well over a hundred online mentions of the park.

Options are plentiful. Jetties, piers, and open shoreline all offer spots to cast a line.

The fishing pier is a highlight. It doubles as a lookout point for wildlife and a relaxing place to spend an afternoon.

Crabbing is another beloved tradition. Some families have been fishing and crabbing here since their own childhood, returning year after year.

The mix of bay and river water gives anglers choices. Many pair a morning of fishing with a picnic later in the day.

Beach fishing is popular too. Shoreline casting lets people enjoy the views while they wait for a bite.

Patience pays off here, and not just in fish. The quiet pace is part of what makes the experience so restful.

Bring your gear and some snacks, and a full day can slip away without notice. For those who prefer paddling to casting, the boat ramp is next.

Paddles In The Inner Bay

Kayakers have a simple routine here. Launch at the boat ramp, paddle the inner bay, then drive over to the beach for a swim.

The launch is described as nice and easy to use. That makes it friendly for beginners and seasoned paddlers alike.

Calm water is the big advantage. The inner bay offers a relaxed paddle without the stress of heavy chop.

Boaters also use the ramp to reach wider waters. With the Potomac on one side and the Chesapeake on the other, there is no shortage of routes.

The beaches themselves are also suited to kayaking. Clear, calm conditions make launching from shore an option as well.

Biking is another way to cover ground. The park has trails that work for cycling or walking.

Getting between camp areas on foot is tricky, though. Camp roads are the practical way to move around.

Paddling past this historic shoreline offers a different view of the land. Sunset, as it turns out, offers yet another.

Sunsets Over The Potomac

Evening may be the park’s best-kept secret. Watching the sun set over the Potomac is often named the part you cannot miss.

The western-facing river shore gives a clear view as daylight fades. Picnickers often time their visit to stay for the show.

After dark, the night sky takes over. Campers stay up to see an incredible number of stars thanks to the remote location.

That combination of sunset and stargazing is a big reason people book overnight stays. It turns a day trip into something more memorable.

For ghost story fans, nightfall adds a certain mood. A dark shoreline on historic ground is the classic setting for a campfire tale.

Photographers find plenty to work with too. Windy days and changing light make for strong pictures around the water and lighthouse.

Arriving later in the day can also mean lighter crowds. One Saturday evening arrival on a holiday weekend came with no traffic at the gate.

Of course, enjoying those stars is easiest if you stay the night. The campgrounds make that simple.

Campsites Tucked In The Trees

Privacy is the word that keeps coming up about camping here. Trees and bay grass separate the sites so well that neighbors can be hard to spot.

Camping draws more than a hundred mentions online. Both tent campers and RV travelers find options.

Newly renovated full hookup sites are available for RVs. The park closed for infrastructure repairs at one point and has since reopened with updates, including new gates.

Bathhouses get high marks. They are large and clean, with hot water and showers.

Check-in is described as easy, and the camp staff are helpful. A small playground in the tent area keeps kids busy.

A few cautions apply. Poison ivy has been reported around some campsites and along a wooded path to the beach, so watch your step.

Free firewood can be found in the woods, but reaching it may mean navigating that poison ivy. Mosquitoes can be strong in marshy camp areas, especially in spring.

Gate keypads may sit low for trucks pulling campers, which is worth knowing on arrival. With a bit of preparation, the sites deliver a quiet, historic overnight.

Hours, Fees, And Pets

Planning ahead is easy because the hours stay consistent. The park is open every day of the week from 7 am to 7 pm.

Entrance fees vary. Out-of-state guests have reported paying $17 at busier times, while one out-of-state visit came in at $5.

Fees can change by season, so checking the Maryland Department of Natural Resources website before your trip is smart. Maryland residents may see different rates.

Dog owners have a reason to smile. A pet beach is one of the park’s talked-about features.

The lighthouse area sells merchandise at fair prices, and purchases support the park. It is a nice way to bring home a souvenir with purpose.

Crowds tend to stay manageable. Even busy days are described as roomy rather than packed.

Pack bug spray, sunscreen, and water shoes. Checking for ticks after trails and camp areas is a good habit.

With those basics covered, all that is left is deciding whether this park lives up to its spooky billing.

A Haunted Title Worth Testing

So, is this the most haunted spot in Maryland? Nobody can hand out an official trophy, but few places have a better claim.

The Civil War prison history is real and well documented. The lighthouse stands as a lasting link to the past, and local legends have grown around both.

What surprises many is how peaceful the park feels today. Calm beaches, private campsites, and sunsets over the Potomac make it a favorite escape.

History lovers get markers and stories. Families get swimming, crabbing, and a playground.

Anglers get piers and jetties, while paddlers get an easy launch and calm inner bay waters. Stargazers get skies full of stars.

Bring bug spray, respect the history, and keep an eye out for jellyfish. Those small steps go a long way.

Whether the ghost stories win you over or not, the trip rarely disappoints. The park’s long list of loyal returners speaks for itself.

Come for the legends, and odds are you will stay for the sunset.
